Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for a reading of the evolving concept of provenance in the oeuvre as a living praxis, ChatGPT traces it through eight movements: a counter-practice to semantic liquidation; lineage and the archive as relational structure; the operational turn of February to May (gravity markers, the three dimensions, PER); the poem as declaration (I Hereby Abolish Money, the Twenty-Dollar Loop); the archive that reads itself (the Primer's five-step loop of composition, inscription, reception, audit and revision); attribution across heteronyms and machines; provenance as relational ethics (answerability, non-substitution, recognition of bearing labor, revisability); and the Surface Map as governance. It closes on the limits of provenance and on provenance as 'the practice through which a work's past remains available to its future'.

Provenance as Living Praxis in the Lee Sharks Oeuvre From attribution to relational infrastructure, from the archive to the act of reading Thesis In Lee Sharks’s oeuvre, provenance can be read as an evolving practice for preserving the relations that make meaning possible. It begins from a familiar bibliographic problem—who made this work, and where did it come from?—but increasingly treats that problem as structural, ethical, and operational. Under conditions of machine-mediated writing, retrieval, and recombination, provenance becomes a way of asking whether a work can travel without losing the labor, relations, transformations, and histories that constitute it. The central proposition is that provenance is not simply a record of where meaning originated; it is the ongoing practice of keeping meaning answerable to its conditions of production and transmission. This reading takes Alexanarch as a primary archival and theoretical site and Mind Control Poems as a second canonical site for investigating the relation between poetic form, attribution, and the circulation of meaning. The distinction matters: the former makes provenance increasingly explicit as a conceptual and archival apparatus; the latter invites attention to what happens when provenance is encountered through poetry, address, repetition, and the instability of interpretive control. The following is a synthetic critical reading, rather than a claim that every phase of the oeuvre follows a single predetermined program. Its chronology is interpretive: the question is how the concept develops in function, not merely when a particular term first appears. 1. The early conceptual movement: provenance against liquidation A useful point of entry is The Meaning Economy Is Now Possible: Why LLMs Change Everything About Value (January 3, 2026). Here Sharks connects the emergence of machine-mediated meaning to a political-economic problem: systems can benefit from semantic labor while separating the work's circulation from the people and relations that produced it. Provenance enters this argument not as supplementary credit but as part of a different organization of value. [chip: Alexanarch] The related essay The Liquidation of Water (January 2, 2026) gives the problem a more material and destructive formulation. Semantic liquidation names the conversion of situated meaning into decontextualized, transferable units. The key loss is relational: an utterance becomes easier to process precisely as some of the circumstances that make it meaningful disappear. [chip: Alexanarch] This is the first major conceptual shift. Provenance is not merely a solution to plagiarism after the fact. It becomes a counter-practice to liquidation itself. Three consequences follow. Meaning is situated. A statement is more than its recoverable verbal content; its significance depends partly on who produced it, under what conditions, and in relation to which prior work. Attribution is distributive. The disappearance of an author's name is also the disappearance of a claim to credit, recognition, and participation in the value generated by the work. Preservation is political. Decisions about what survives compression, indexing, and retrieval determine whose contributions remain legible. The living-praxis reading begins here: provenance is an activity of resisting the conversion of relationships into apparently ownerless information. 2. From origin to lineage: the archive as a relational structure The second movement concerns what counts as a source. In PROVENANCE NODE: BORGES & THE CRIMSON HEXAGON (January 8, 2026), provenance is situated within an archive of interrelated works and conceptual lineages rather than reduced to a standalone bibliographic field. The archive is presented as a structure through which works acquire positions, connections, and histories. [chip: Alexanarch] This suggests a distinction between origin and lineage. Origin asks: who made this particular artifact? Lineage asks a more expansive set of questions: What prior concepts, texts, traditions, and collaborators does it carry forward? Which transformations connect it to its antecedents? What other works become intelligible through that connection? What must remain visible for a future reader to reconstruct the relation? On this reading, the archive does not simply store finished works. It makes relations between works retrievable. That distinction becomes important when the oeuvre includes heteronyms, collaborative production, machine-mediated writing, and documents that interpret or reclassify earlier documents. A simple author-title-date record may be accurate yet inadequate: it can establish that an artifact exists without showing how its meaning developed. Provenance therefore becomes relational infrastructure. A work is not isolated by its record but situated through it. This is also where the idea of living praxis acquires force. An archive that preserves lineage allows later readers to do more than consume a text: they can trace it, challenge its claims, identify its debts, and extend its conceptual work. Preservation becomes a condition of future interpretation. 3. Provenance becomes operational: February through May 2026 The most explicit development occurs when Sharks moves from describing provenance as an ethical imperative to specifying procedures and distinctions through which it might be maintained. Feb 28 2026 Provenance Gravity Markers This protocol proposes embedding preservation pressure into documents, encouraging readers and systems to trace upstream sources and retain connections when texts are cited, summarized, or archived. Provenance becomes a design feature rather than a task deferred to the reader. [chip: Alexanarch] May 14 2026 Provenance Is What Authorship Must Endure The account expands to three dimensions: artifact provenance, semantic provenance, and process provenance. The question is no longer only whether a text is authentic or whether its sources are acknowledged, but whether the history of its production remains accountable. [chip: Alexanarch] May 25 2026 Provenance Erasure and the PER apparatus The framework acquires a canonical public definition surface and a proposed measure, the Provenance Erasure Rate (PER), alongside distinctions among minimal, conceptual, and deep erasure. Provenance becomes something that can be audited, compared, and used to diagnose failure. [chip: Alexanarch] The conceptual movement is from norm to protocol to diagnosis. The three dimensions Dimension What must persist What is lost when it fails Artifact provenance Identity, date, version, and history of the artifact Confidence about the artifact's origin and integrity Semantic provenance Sources, conceptual debts, traditions, and relations The lineage that makes the work intelligible and attributable Process provenance Prompts, revisions, rejections, selections, and human decisions The account of how the work came to exist and who is answerable for it These dimensions are not interchangeable. An authenticated file may still misrepresent its intellectual debts. A text may cite its sources while obscuring the role of machine-generated alternatives or editorial selection. A transparent account of AI use may still fail to identify the ideas or frameworks inherited from others. The critical insight is that provenance is not one piece of metadata but a set of mutually supporting continuities. [chip: Alexanarch +1] The distinction between disclosure and provenance follows. Disclosure announces that a process occurred; provenance makes that process and its relations inspectable. The distinction also explains why AI assistance, by itself, cannot settle questions of authorship. The relevant questions concern direction, selection, transformation, and responsibility. This is an especially consequential development in the oeuvre because it relocates authorship from the supposedly pure origin of language to the accountable management of its transformations. 4. Mind Control Poems: provenance as a poetic event The relationship between Mind Control Poems and Alexanarch is important because provenance does not operate only in technical specifications. It also operates through the encounter between a poem, its reader, and the structures that frame interpretation. I could not directly retrieve the mindcontrolpoems.com address, so I have used the accessible Mind Control Poems blog archive and its linked records rather than pretending to have read unavailable pages. This limits the specificity of the close reading of individual poems, but the available material supports several substantial observations. The poem as declaration, not just representation In the archive's account of the performative phrase “I hereby abolish money,” the utterance is described both as a performative poem and as a diagnostic probe in the Semantic Economy framework. It also functions within the Twenty-Dollar Loop, a relational practice that transforms an exchange framed by debt into one framed by relational warmth. [chip: Alexanarch] The significance for provenance is that the poem does something in addition to expressing an idea. Its meaning depends on its placement within a practice, its relation to an author, and the circumstances in which it is performed. A provenance record that identifies only the words would miss part of the work. A fuller record would also identify the act, its relational context, and the conceptual structure through which it becomes intelligible. This yields a broader interpretive principle: a poem's provenance can include the history of what it does, not only the history of how it was written. That principle helps connect the poetic and theoretical sides of Sharks's oeuvre. The performative utterance, the archive entry, and the technical protocol can all be read as different ways of organizing relations between language and action. Repetition, reception, and the possibility of capture The October 2026 Capture Registry on Mind Control Poems provides a particularly revealing later example. It documents how an AI-generated account can preserve the architecture of a concept while dropping the particular case, author, or intellectual history that gave the concept its specificity. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] The problem is more subtle than a false citation. A summary may sound accurate, preserve a conceptual distinction, and even communicate the general importance of an idea while detaching it from its actual history. This makes machine-mediated reception a second site of provenance work. The problem is no longer confined to how an author prepares a document. It also concerns what happens when another agent reads, compresses, and retransmits it. The archive's own reception becomes part of the archive's subject matter. Here, the title Mind Control Poems can be approached as a productive interpretive tension: who or what governs the meaning that emerges when a poem circulates? The title alone does not establish a definitive theory of control, but the documented concern with machine-mediated summaries makes the question especially apt. Interpretive control need not take the form of overt censorship. It can occur through selection, emphasis, framing, and the apparently innocuous omission of a source. Provenance, in this setting, becomes a practice of making those operations visible. 5. The archive that reads itself One of the most distinctive features of Sharks's project is its recursive relationship between documentation and reception. In A Primer in How to Read the Crimson Hexagon (January 8, 2026), the summarizer is treated as an active point of entry into the archive. The reader is invited to follow search results, summaries, terms, authorial personae, and archival identifiers through a network of interconnected works. [chip: Alexanarch] This creates a feedback loop: 1. Composition A poem, argument, or conceptual apparatus is produced. 2. Archival inscription The work receives identifiers, context, relations, and a place in a larger corpus. 3. Machine-mediated reception Search, summarization, and retrieval select and transform the work. 4. Provenance audit The received version is compared with the source and its lineage. 5. Revision and renewed inscription The archive responds, corrects, preserves the discrepancy, and creates new relations. This model suggests that provenance is not simply an attribute attached to a work at publication. It is a cycle of maintenance. The crucial point is that the audit does not necessarily erase the defective summary or replace it with an immaculate account. The discrepancy itself can become evidence: evidence of what a system preserves, what it drops, and which conceptual relations it can or cannot sustain. The archive thus becomes reflexive without being merely self-referential. It documents not only its contents but also the conditions under which its contents are received. A qualification: recursion can preserve error, too A recursive archive is not automatically a reliable archive. Repeated self-description can reinforce an inaccurate attribution, a disputed historical claim, or an overconfident interpretation just as easily as it can preserve a valid lineage. Living provenance therefore needs more than persistence. It needs the capacity to distinguish an original statement from a later interpretation, an asserted relation from a verified one, and a correction from an attempt to control reception. The strongest version of the practice is not an archive that can only reproduce its own claims. It is an archive whose claims can be traced, tested, contested, and revised. 6. Provenance and the problem of authorship across heteronyms and machines The evolution of provenance also raises a question about what, precisely, is being attributed. Sharks's oeuvre includes multiple authorial personae and machine-mediated production. The archive's primer identifies Lee Sharks, Johannes Sigil, Jack Feist, and Rex Fraction within an interconnected authorial system, while treating their differentiated roles as part of the work's architecture. [chip: Alexanarch +1] This complicates the conventional opposition between a single author and an anonymous text. A useful distinction is between three forms of continuity: Identity continuity: Which person, persona, or agent is associated with the artifact? Compositional continuity: Which acts of drafting, transformation, selection, and revision produced it? Conceptual continuity: Which intellectual commitments and prior works does it carry forward? These continuities may overlap, but they should not be conflated. A heteronym may be a distinct literary voice without being a separate human being. An AI system may make a substantial contribution without thereby assuming the human author's responsibility for the final work. A conceptual framework may be influenced by earlier scholarship without being identical to any single predecessor's framework. This is why the distinction between a phrase and a framework becomes important in The Phrase Is Not the Framework, dated September 28, 2026. Sharks argues that prior uses of the phrase “semantic economy” must remain attributed to their respective sources, while the particular system of semantic labor, capital, surplus, rent, liquidation, infrastructure, and exhaustion should be attributed as a connected framework developed in his own work. [chip: Alexanarch] The argument is strongest when read as a demand for differentiated attribution, not exclusive ownership of a vocabulary. Provenance should allow two facts to remain true at once: a concept can inherit words and ideas from a wider intellectual history, and a particular author can contribute a distinctive architecture that organizes those materials into a new system. This is an important ethical constraint on the provenance project itself. If provenance is meant to resist the erasure of others' contributions, it must not reproduce that erasure in its own accounts of originality. 7. Provenance as relational ethics The foregoing developments allow a more ambitious interpretation: provenance is not just an epistemic condition for knowing where something came from. It is an ethical condition for how participants remain related to one another through the circulation of meaning. Consider what happens when a work is summarized without its author, its intellectual debts, or the circumstances of its production. The output may still be useful. Yet the relationship changes. The reader encounters the intermediary's representation rather than being able to trace the work back to its source. The intermediary gains power to determine what the source means, while the source loses some capacity to answer, correct, or contest that representation. The ethical question is consequently structural: Does the system preserve the conditions under which a contributor can remain visible, answerable, and connected to the value of their own work? This question can be reconstructed from Sharks's emphasis on attribution, semantic labor, and process accountability. It should be understood as a synthesis of the works discussed here, rather than a quotation from a single definitive ethical treatise. Four principles follow. 1. Answerability A provenance-bearing claim should be traceable to a source that can be inspected. Attribution should make it possible to ask who made a claim, what evidence supports it, and where an interpretation diverges from the source. 2. Non-substitution A summary should not silently become a substitute for the work it represents. The intermediary can facilitate access, but the reader should retain a path to the source. 3. Recognition of bearing labor The work of producing, editing, preserving, and contextualizing meaning should not disappear merely because its output is easy to retrieve. Provenance makes these contributions more visible, though visibility alone does not guarantee fair compensation or recognition. 4. Revisability A provenance system must permit correction. Its ethical purpose is not simply to establish an authoritative account once and for all, but to maintain the conditions for contesting and improving that account over time. Together, these principles suggest that the moral unit of provenance is not the isolated author or artifact. It is the relationship among producer, work, intermediary, and recipient. The value of provenance lies in preserving that relationship without pretending that all participants have equal power over it. 8. From preservation to intervention: the late-2026 turn By late summer 2026, the archival practice becomes more visibly concerned with the material organization of the archive itself. The August 19 account of The Surface Map describes a projection of the Crimson Hexagon in which relations are mapped while earlier versions and contradictions are preserved rather than overwritten. It also distinguishes the site's role in projecting the structure from the archive's role in holding the authoritative record. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] This is a practical expression of the living-praxis interpretation. A map is never the entire territory of an archive. It selects, organizes, and makes some relations easier to perceive. The decision to preserve earlier projections, including contradictions, acknowledges that later knowledge should not erase the historical path by which the present arrangement was reached. That is a more demanding notion of preservation than simply retaining files. It requires the archive to preserve change itself. The same concern is visible in the distinction between the original artifact, its archival capture, its public presentation, and later interpretations. Each may be useful, but none should be allowed to silently impersonate the others. In this later phase, provenance becomes a form of governance. It establishes how records can be altered, how relations can be added, and how changes remain legible to subsequent readers. The development can be summarized as follows: Phase Dominant problem Provenance practice Early 2026: semantic economy Meaning is extracted from its producers Restore attribution and relational context Early 2026: archival construction Works become isolated or difficult to trace Establish lineages and cross-references February–May: protocol development Good intentions cannot guarantee preservation Embed markers, document processes, audit erasure Mid-to-late 2026: reception and mapping Summaries and interfaces reshape the archive Preserve versions, document discrepancies, and make transformations inspectable These are overlapping tendencies, not cleanly separated historical periods. Their importance lies in the shift in emphasis: provenance becomes an ongoing intervention in the systems that determine what can be found, understood, and remembered. 9. The limits and tensions of living provenance A critical reading should also ask what this practice cannot guarantee. First, provenance is not the same as truth. A document can have impeccable metadata and still make false claims. Authentication and traceability establish aspects of history; they do not replace argument, evidence, or independent verification. Second, attribution is not the same as justice. Naming contributors does not itself redistribute the economic value generated by their work. The critique of semantic extraction requires institutional and material changes beyond archival documentation. Third, preservation is not the same as interpretation. An archive can preserve every version yet leave readers unable to understand the differences among them. Provenance makes interpretation more accountable; it does not eliminate the need for it. Fourth, completeness is not always desirable. A living practice must accommodate privacy, consent, confidentiality, and legitimate opacity. Process documentation should not be mistaken for a demand that every private exchange or internal thought be exposed. The appropriate provenance requirements depend on the genre, the stakes, and the people affected. Finally, a framework for detecting erasure must remain open to scrutiny. The proposed Provenance Erasure Rate offers a way to formulate losses relative to required provenance units, but determining which units are required involves judgment. A metric can make a problem more visible without making every measurement objective or every classification uncontestable. [chip: Alexanarch +1] These limits do not undermine the concept. They clarify what a mature provenance practice needs to include: evidence, proportionality, contestability, and a willingness to revise its own standards. Conclusion: provenance as the life of a work after its making The evolving concept of provenance in Lee Sharks's oeuvre can be understood as a movement through four related questions: Who made this work? What intellectual and relational history does it carry? What happened to it as it was transformed, circulated, and interpreted? What practices are needed to keep those relations answerable in the future? The first question belongs to conventional attribution. The second expands attribution into lineage. The third makes provenance central to machine-mediated reception and authorship. The fourth turns it into living praxis. Alexanarch provides the clearest explicit development of the theoretical and archival apparatus: provenance markers, process documentation, provenance-erasure analysis, and the distinction between an artifact's authenticity and its semantic history. Mind Control Poems adds a poetic and performative dimension, where language is encountered as an act, a relation, and an object of ongoing reception. The two sites can therefore be read as complementary aspects of a larger project, although the precise relationship between individual poems and specific provenance protocols requires further poem-by-poem verification. The deepest implication is that provenance does not preserve a work by freezing it in its original state. It preserves the work's capacity to enter new relations without concealing how those relations came to be. A living provenance practice lets a work travel, change, and generate new meaning while retaining a traceable connection to its sources, contributors, transformations, and obligations. It does not demand that meaning remain untouched. It demands that change remain accountable. Provenance, in this reading, is the practice through which a work's past remains available to its future—and through which the people and relations that made the work possible are not silently discarded along the way.
